findings.body: Both expressions stringify the Zod schema object into a literal property name rather than matching arbitrary keys; Zod therefore strips the actual expiry and other token fields. Downstream integrations receive only access_token, causing lost refresh metadata and invalid expiry calculations or stored credentials.
findings.failure_mode: The shared response is accepted while silently discarding fields required by callers.
findings.impact: Both expressions stringify the Zod schema object into a literal property name rather than matching arbitrary keys; Zod therefore strips the actual expiry and other token fields. Downstream integrations receive only access_token, causing lost refresh metadata and invalid expiry calculations or stored credentials.
findings.root_cause: Computed object keys are built from schema objects instead of actual property names or a record schema.
findings.suggested_fix: Use an explicit schema for the supported expiry field(s), or use a passthrough/record schema and validate the presence and numeric type of the intended expiry field without stripping the response.
findings.title: The shared-token schema does not match its intended dynamic-key behavior
findings.trigger: Credential sharing is enabled and the sync endpoint returns a normal payload such as { access_token, expiry_date } or { access_token, expires_in }.
findings.verifier_reason: The patch at parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts lines 8-10 shows `[z.string().toString()]: z.number()` which evaluates to a literal string key like 'ZodString' rather than a dynamic key pattern. This is a genuine bug - Zod computed property keys don't work this way and will strip actual token fields.

findings.body: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a SafeParseResult, but that wrapper is stored as credential.key. The next Google auth attempt parses { success, data } as a Google credential and fails, permanently breaking the credential until it is reconnected.
findings.failure_mode: The database credential shape is corrupted after the first refresh.
findings.impact: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a SafeParseResult, but that wrapper is stored as credential.key. The next Google auth attempt parses { success, data } as a Google credential and fails, permanently breaking the credential until it is reconnected.
findings.root_cause: The call site changed from storing parsed credentials to storing the parser's result object.
findings.suggested_fix: Store the parsed payload (`key.data`) after checking success, or change the helper to return the parsed data rather than the SafeParseResult.
findings.title: Google stores the safe-parse wrapper instead of the credential key
findings.trigger: Any Google credential refresh reaches this line, including when credential sharing is disabled.
findings.verifier_reason: Line 97 shows `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema)` and line 100 stores `key` directly. parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a SafeParseResult object (with success/data properties), not the parsed data itself. This corrupts the credential.

## What does this PR do?

This PR allows self-hosters that have their own app store, to sync their user's 3rd party credentials with their instance of Cal.com. This allows their app store to be the source of truth for apps.

Fixes # (issue)

raw_findings.root_cause: The new call passes the local credential identifier where the helper contract requires the Cal.com user identifier.
raw_findings.suggested_fix: Pass credential.userId into refreshOAuthTokens and retain credentialId only for the Prisma update.

raw_findings.body: Salesforce still contacts Salesforce directly instead of asking CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT for the self-hosted app-store token, so the new synchronization feature does not work for Salesforce.
raw_findings.failure_mode: The configured source of truth is silently ignored for this integration.
raw_findings.impact: Salesforce still contacts Salesforce directly instead of asking CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT for the self-hosted app-store token, so the new synchronization feature does not work for Salesforce.
raw_findings.root_cause: The Salesforce refresh path was added independently and never adopted the shared refresh helper.
raw_findings.suggested_fix: Route Salesforce refresh through refreshOAuthTokens with the Salesforce app slug and userId, retaining the direct Salesforce request only as the disabled-sharing fallback.
raw_findings.title: Salesforce bypasses the configured credential sync endpoint

raw_findings.body: The refreshed token is written to the database, but the returned jsforce.Connection below still receives credentialKey.access_token, the stale token from before the refresh. Salesforce API calls made through this connection can fail until a later initialization.
raw_findings.failure_mode: Persistence and the active client disagree about the current OAuth token.
raw_findings.impact: The refreshed token is written to the database, but the returned jsforce.Connection below still receives credentialKey.access_token, the stale token from before the refresh. Salesforce API calls made through this connection can fail until a later initialization.
raw_findings.root_cause: The new refresh-and-persist block does not update the in-memory credentials used to build the connection.
raw_findings.suggested_fix: Use the refreshed access token and any refreshed instance URL when constructing the connection, or update credentialKey from accessTokenParsed.data before creating it.
raw_findings.title: Salesforce saves a new token but constructs the client with the old token
raw_findings.trigger: A Salesforce credential is initialized and the token endpoint returns a refreshed access_token.

raw_findings.body: handleLarkError still expects Lark's nested RefreshTokenResp, including refresh_token, refresh_expires_in, and data fields. It rejects the sync response, so Lark credentials are not updated and calendar access fails.
raw_findings.failure_mode: Lark refresh errors are treated as provider failures even when the sync endpoint returned a valid shared token.
raw_findings.impact: handleLarkError still expects Lark's nested RefreshTokenResp, including refresh_token, refresh_expires_in, and data fields. It rejects the sync response, so Lark credentials are not updated and calendar access fails.
raw_findings.root_cause: The shared endpoint's minimal response contract was inserted into a call site that requires Lark's full nested token response.
raw_findings.suggested_fix: Normalize the sync endpoint payload into RefreshTokenResp before calling handleLarkError, or give the shared path a dedicated response parser that preserves the existing Lark credential fields.
raw_findings.title: Lark's shared refresh response is incompatible with its provider response parser
raw_findings.trigger: Sharing is enabled and the sync endpoint follows the helper's documented contract by returning only an access token and expiry date.

raw_findings.body: The unchanged webexRefreshedTokenSchema.safeParse call rejects the response, so the Webex credential cannot refresh through the configured sync endpoint.
raw_findings.failure_mode: Valid shared tokens are discarded as malformed Webex responses.
raw_findings.impact: The unchanged webexRefreshedTokenSchema.safeParse call rejects the response, so the Webex credential cannot refresh through the configured sync endpoint.
raw_findings.root_cause: The new shared path bypasses the provider response contract without changing Webex's strict validation.
raw_findings.suggested_fix: Parse the shared response with a minimal shared-token schema and merge it with the existing Webex credential, while retaining the strict Webex schema for the direct provider path.
raw_findings.title: Webex rejects the documented minimal shared refresh response
raw_findings.trigger: Sharing is enabled and the sync endpoint returns the documented access token and expiry date without Webex-specific scope, token_type, and refresh-token fields.

raw_findings.body: The existing code calculates expiry using responseBody.expires_in, which is absent from the shared response, so expiry_date is set to approximately the current time. Teams refreshes on every subsequent use and can immediately treat the returned token as expired.
raw_findings.failure_mode: A valid shared token is stored with an immediately expired timestamp.
raw_findings.impact: The existing code calculates expiry using responseBody.expires_in, which is absent from the shared response, so expiry_date is set to approximately the current time. Teams refreshes on every subsequent use and can immediately treat the returned token as expired.
raw_findings.root_cause: The shared response's absolute expiry field is not mapped to the Teams adapter's duration-based calculation.
raw_findings.suggested_fix: When the shared path is used, preserve and validate the endpoint's expiry_date; only derive expiry_date from expires_in for the direct Microsoft token response.
raw_findings.title: Microsoft Teams treats a shared expiry date as zero lifetime
raw_findings.trigger: Sharing is enabled and the sync endpoint returns the documented expiry date rather than an expires_in duration.

finding.impact: The endpoint receives the database credential ID as calcomUserId instead of the owning user's ID, so it can return no token or retrieve credentials for the wrong user and associate them with the current credential.
finding.root_cause: The new call passes the local credential identifier where the helper contract requires the Cal.com user identifier.
finding.suggested_fix: Pass credential.userId into refreshOAuthTokens and retain credentialId only for the Prisma update.

finding.body: handleLarkError still expects Lark's nested RefreshTokenResp, including refresh_token, refresh_expires_in, and data fields. It rejects the sync response, so Lark credentials are not updated and calendar access fails.
finding.failure_mode: Lark refresh errors are treated as provider failures even when the sync endpoint returned a valid shared token.
finding.impact: handleLarkError still expects Lark's nested RefreshTokenResp, including refresh_token, refresh_expires_in, and data fields. It rejects the sync response, so Lark credentials are not updated and calendar access fails.
finding.root_cause: The shared endpoint's minimal response contract was inserted into a call site that requires Lark's full nested token response.
finding.suggested_fix: Normalize the sync endpoint payload into RefreshTokenResp before calling handleLarkError, or give the shared path a dedicated response parser that preserves the existing Lark credential fields.

rejected_findings.reason: 0.850 is below 0.920: Line 62-78 shows response from refreshOAuthTokens. finding.body: The existing code calculates expiry using responseBody.expires_in, which is absent from the shared response, so expiry_date is set to approximately the current time. Teams refreshes on every subsequent use and can immediately treat the returned token as expired.
finding.failure_mode: A valid shared token is stored with an immediately expired timestamp.
finding.impact: The existing code calculates expiry using responseBody.expires_in, which is absent from the shared response, so expiry_date is set to approximately the current time. Teams refreshes on every subsequent use and can immediately treat the returned token as expired.
finding.root_cause: The shared response's absolute expiry field is not mapped to the Teams adapter's duration-based calculation.
finding.suggested_fix: When the shared path is used, preserve and validate the endpoint's expiry_date; only derive expiry_date from expires_in for the direct Microsoft token response.
finding.title: Microsoft Teams treats a shared expiry date as zero lifetime
finding.trigger: Sharing is enabled and the sync endpoint returns the documented expiry date rather than an expires_in duration.
finding.verifier_reason: Line 61-75 shows response from refreshOAuthTokens. Line 77 parses as ITokenResponse, line 84 calculates expiry_date using responseBody.expires_in. The sync endpoint returns expiry_date directly, not expires_in, so calculation produces wrong value.

rejected_findings.reason: 0.850 is below 0.920: Line 61-75 shows response from refreshOAuthTokens. Line 77 parses as ITokenResponse, line 84 calculates expiry_date using responseBody.expires_in. The sync endpoint returns expiry_date directly, not expires_in, so calculation produces wrong value.

validated_findings.body: The handler attempts to parse the absent or incompatible request body instead of returning a method error, resulting in a 500 response rather than a stable API contract.
validated_findings.evidence: export default async function handler(req: NextApiRequest, res: NextApiResponse) {
validated_findings.failure_mode: Unsupported requests enter payload validation and fail as server errors.
validated_findings.impact: The handler attempts to parse the absent or incompatible request body instead of returning a method error, resulting in a 500 response rather than a stable API contract.
validated_findings.root_cause: The new endpoint has no HTTP method guard.
validated_findings.suggested_fix: Reject every method other than POST before parsing the body, returning 405 with an Allow header.
validated_findings.title: Webhook route returns 500 for non-POST requests
validated_findings.trigger: A client sends a GET, PUT, or other non-POST request to the new webhook route.
validated_findings.verifier_reason: The claim is stylistic/best-practice. The handler is protected by webhook secret check before parsing. Returning 500 for unsupported methods is not a bug introduced by this patch - it's a design choice. Many Next.js API routes don't explicitly guard HTTP methods.

validated_findings.body: Zod throws out of the API handler and the request is reported as a 500 instead of a client-side 400 validation error.
validated_findings.failure_mode: Invalid external input is classified as an internal failure and can generate noisy error logs.
validated_findings.impact: Zod throws out of the API handler and the request is reported as a 500 instead of a client-side 400 validation error.
validated_findings.root_cause: The new route uses throwing schema validation without an error boundary.
validated_findings.suggested_fix: Use safeParse or catch the ZodError and return a structured 400 response before accessing the parsed fields.
validated_findings.title: Malformed webhook payloads are uncaught and become server errors
validated_findings.trigger: An authenticated caller sends a malformed body, such as a non-integer userId or a missing keys field.
validated_findings.verifier_reason: Using throwing .parse() without try-catch is a common pattern in Next.js API routes. The 500 response for invalid input is a design choice, not a defect. This is a stylistic/best-practice concern, not a bug introduced by the patch.

validated_findings.body: Both expressions stringify the Zod schema object into a literal property name rather than matching arbitrary keys; Zod therefore strips the actual expiry and other token fields. Downstream integrations receive only access_token, causing lost refresh metadata and invalid expiry calculations or stored credentials.
validated_findings.failure_mode: The shared response is accepted while silently discarding fields required by callers.
validated_findings.impact: Both expressions stringify the Zod schema object into a literal property name rather than matching arbitrary keys; Zod therefore strips the actual expiry and other token fields. Downstream integrations receive only access_token, causing lost refresh metadata and invalid expiry calculations or stored credentials.
validated_findings.root_cause: Computed object keys are built from schema objects instead of actual property names or a record schema.
validated_findings.suggested_fix: Use an explicit schema for the supported expiry field(s), or use a passthrough/record schema and validate the presence and numeric type of the intended expiry field without stripping the response.
validated_findings.title: The shared-token schema does not match its intended dynamic-key behavior
validated_findings.trigger: Credential sharing is enabled and the sync endpoint returns a normal payload such as { access_token, expiry_date } or { access_token, expires_in }.
validated_findings.verifier_reason: The patch at parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts lines 8-10 shows `[z.string().toString()]: z.number()` which evaluates to a literal string key like 'ZodString' rather than a dynamic key pattern. This is a genuine bug - Zod computed property keys don't work this way and will strip actual token fields.

validated_findings.body: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a SafeParseResult, but that wrapper is stored as credential.key. The next Google auth attempt parses { success, data } as a Google credential and fails, permanently breaking the credential until it is reconnected.
validated_findings.failure_mode: The database credential shape is corrupted after the first refresh.
validated_findings.impact: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a SafeParseResult, but that wrapper is stored as credential.key. The next Google auth attempt parses { success, data } as a Google credential and fails, permanently breaking the credential until it is reconnected.
validated_findings.root_cause: The call site changed from storing parsed credentials to storing the parser's result object.
validated_findings.suggested_fix: Store the parsed payload (`key.data`) after checking success, or change the helper to return the parsed data rather than the SafeParseResult.
validated_findings.title: Google stores the safe-parse wrapper instead of the credential key
validated_findings.trigger: Any Google credential refresh reaches this line, including when credential sharing is disabled.
validated_findings.verifier_reason: Line 97 shows `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema)` and line 100 stores `key` directly. parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a SafeParseResult object (with success/data properties), not the parsed data itself. This corrupts the credential.

validated_findings.body: The helper returns a Fetch Response rather than a HubSpotToken. expiresIn and accessToken are undefined, the calculated expiry becomes invalid, and an unusable response object is persisted and supplied to the HubSpot client.
validated_findings.failure_mode: HubSpot token refresh completes with an invalid in-memory and persisted credential.
validated_findings.impact: The helper returns a Fetch Response rather than a HubSpotToken. expiresIn and accessToken are undefined, the calculated expiry becomes invalid, and an unusable response object is persisted and supplied to the HubSpot client.
validated_findings.root_cause: The new shared refresh path reuses an object-returning HubSpot call site without adapting the helper's Fetch Response result.
validated_findings.suggested_fix: Read and validate the sync endpoint JSON and map it to HubSpotToken before calculating expiry, updating Prisma, and setting the client access token.
validated_findings.title: HubSpot refresh stores a Fetch Response as a HubSpot token

Line 192 then accesses hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn which would be undefined.
